catalog_citation: Wilkins, David P. 1989. Mparntwe Arrernte (Aranda): studies in the structure and semantics of grammar. PhD thesis, Australian National University (ANU Open Research hdl 1885/9908).
catalog_quote: 2.2 Stress. The assignment of stress (primary, secondary, clitics, etc.) in Mparntwe Arrernte is not entirely clear, and deserves fuller investigation. One rule that covers a large number of lexemes, is that stress is assigned to the first syllable which is opened by a consonant. (26) ineme /inəmə/ [inə́mɐ] 'is getting'; neme /nəmə/ [nə́mɐ] 'is sitting'. One source of counter-examples to this rule appears to arise when there is an initial /a/ and the second vowel is /ə/. Some words meeting this description may have stress on either the /a/ or the /ə/. The name Arrernte /arəṇṭə/ itself may be realised as either [árəṇḍɐ] or [arə́ṇḍɐ]. Other words may have stress only on the /a/, such as ampwe 'old' [ámbwɐ], or only on the /ə/, such as artwe 'man' [aʼṭwɐ́]. audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding passage is verbatim at Wilkins 1989 section 2.2, printed pp.94-95 = PDF pp.123-124 of the ANU scan we hold (scanned files and page-image crop both opened). (2) Deciding source: a 665-pp reference grammar (1989 ANU PhD), the standard description, but its stress section is brief and author-hedged. (3) downloaded now: Breen & Dobson 2005 JIPA 'Central Arrernte' (open on Cambridge Core), p.252: 'primary stress is normally on the second (underlying) syllable; thus at the surface it falls on the first vowel that follows a consonant' — independently confirms the onset-conditioned left-edge coding (classification weight-hedged, what counts as heavy: onset-or-other, edge left) and adds secondary-stress and exception detail (V-initial monosyllables; shift to initial non-schwa vowel before intervocalic tap, matching Wilkins' [árəɳɖɐ]~[arə́ɳɖɐ]); it points to Henderson 1998:215-221 for the fullest account.

sources.quote: 'In citation forms, primary stress is normally on the second (underlying) syllable; thus at the surface it falls on the first vowel that follows a consonant (even if that vowel is not phonemic). For most speakers of this dialect stress on a monosyllable with an initial vowel at the surface falls on that vowel ... There is a tendency also for stress to move to an initial (non-schwa) vowel if the following consonant is intervocalic /ɾ/. A secondary stress may fall on the second syllable of a bound morpheme, and on the middle syllable of any sequence of three which do not acquire stress from eith
